Install Quarto to a user-local directory

Source: R/quarto-check.R
install_quarto.Rd

Downloads the official Quarto release for this OS from quarto-dev/quarto-cli's GitHub release distribution and installs it to a user-local directory (via tools::R_user_dir(), no admin rights required), matching the ~/opt/quarto-* pattern this package's reference implementation used on Posit Workbench, where the system Quarto is pinned to an old version and users can't install system-wide.

Usage

install_quarto(version = "latest", dir = NULL, force = FALSE)

Arguments

version

Character. Quarto version to install, such as "1.10.18", or "latest" (the default) for the newest stable release. Looking up the newest release needs an internet connection; if that fails, the message says so, and you can name a version yourself instead.

dir

Character or NULL. The folder to install into, created if it does not exist. NULL (the default) uses the folder onepagr manages under tools::R_user_dir(). On Windows this is where the installer is saved; the installer itself asks where to put Quarto.

force

Logical. FALSE (the default) stops when the Quarto onepagr would use is already as new as version. TRUE installs anyway.

Value

Character, the install directory (macOS/Linux) or the downloaded installer path (Windows), invisibly; NULL, invisibly, if you decline the download or the Quarto you have is already new enough.

Details

This function is NEVER called automatically by any other onepagr function; it must be invoked directly by the user, matching the precedent set by reticulate::install_miniconda() and keras::install_keras(). It downloads from an official GitHub release URL over HTTPS only.

On Windows, this downloads the official .msi installer and opens it for the user to complete; Windows installers are not silently run by this function, to avoid requiring elevated-privilege automation. On macOS and Linux, the release archive is downloaded and extracted directly into the user-local install directory.

On Linux the build for the machine's architecture is downloaded (amd64 or arm64). The archive is extracted into quarto-<version>/ under the install directory and the bin/quarto binary is located inside it, so the different archive layouts per platform do not matter.

By default the newest stable Quarto release is installed. It is looked up from the release list at https://api.github.com/repos/quarto-dev/quarto-cli/releases/latest, which leaves out releases still in testing. Quarto 1.10.18 is the first release that bundles Typst 0.15.1, the version onepagr is built and tested against, and a newer Quarto release does not bundle an older Typst, so the newest stable release always meets check_quarto()'s minimum. An older version than 1.10.18 is still installed if you ask for it, with a warning.

By default the install goes into a folder onepagr manages for you (tools::R_user_dir()). Pass dir to install somewhere else, such as a shared /opt folder: the release is unpacked into quarto-<version>/ inside it, next to any other copies, and you need write permission there (if you do not have it, the function stops before downloading and says so). A folder you chose is never cleaned up: older quarto-<version> copies in it are listed and left alone, because they may belong to someone else.

Before it downloads anything, the function looks at the Quarto onepagr would use now (the QUARTO_PATH environment variable, set in the session or in ~/.Renviron, or else the PATH). If that Quarto is already as new as the version you asked for, nothing is installed and the message says where it is; set force = TRUE to install anyway, for example to put a copy in dir. If the requested version is already unpacked in the install folder, it is reused instead of downloaded again.

In an interactive session it asks before the download, which is large (roughly 100 to 250 MB depending on the system); answering no installs nothing. After a successful install into the default folder it removes the older copies it put there before (the quarto-<version> folders, and any older installer or archive left there), so the folder does not grow with every version. It never removes a copy that QUARTO_PATH points into, in this session or in ~/.Renviron, and it never touches a file or folder whose name does not match what it creates.

Examples

if (FALSE) { # \dontrun{
# Never run automatically: downloads ~100+ MB and (on Windows) opens
# an installer. Only ever run this yourself, deliberately.
install_quarto()

# A specific release, instead of the newest:
install_quarto(version = "1.10.18")

# Into a shared folder you can write to, even if another Quarto is
# already on the machine:
install_quarto(dir = "/opt", force = TRUE)
} # }
